Don’t Scapegoat Pete Hegseth

Washington has a familiar ritual after a bad election: find someone to blame whose name wasn’t on the ballot. This month that name is Pete Hegseth.  Secretary Hegseth has been highly effective and President Trump should keep him leading the Department of War.

I haven’t agreed with every decision this administration has made. The Constitution gives Congress the power to take the nation to war. It's not unprecedented for a President to wage war without Congressional authorization, but it is unconstitutional. I said so when our forces went into Iran without a declaration or an authorization, and I still believe it.

Nevertheless, the Secretary of War doesn’t decide whether America goes to war; he executes the mission. Making Secretary Hegseth the fall guy for a duty Congress shirked and President Trump made is wrong.

Judge Mr. Hegseth on the job he was given. He has restored the military’s sense of purpose. Under the previous administration, the Pentagon called climate change an existential threat and poured energy into diversity bureaucracies and ideological training. The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs told Congress he wanted to understand “white rage.” As a West Point graduate, I found it insulting and counterproductive. It told our warriors their own Department saw them through the lens of grievance. It took their service for granted, ignored their mission, and compromised readiness.

Mr. Hegseth swiftly pivoted the Department back to readiness, standards and the warrior ethos. Lethality is the mission, merit is the measure, and the military exists to deter wars and win the ones it must fight. Recruiting, which collapsed in 2022 and 2023, has roared back. Every active-duty branch met its goal for fiscal 2026, most of them months early, and the Army Reserve hit its target for the first time in a decade. Young Americans want to join a military that knows its purpose and is focused on excellence.

Speaking of readiness, this team is tackling the Pentagon’s broken procurement culture. They are replacing the siloed program offices that have run major weapons programs for decades with portfolio executives who own outcomes and have the authority to move money and people to get them. They are tying rewards to delivering on time and on budget and warning big contractors that those who can’t deliver will lose work to those who can. Washington has promised acquisition reform for 30 years. This Secretary is doing it. Congress must align the budget with these reforms, not to fire the reformer.

Has he made mistakes? Yes. The plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution was one. Hasan murdered 13 people at Fort Hood, and he deserves the sentence a military court imposed, but a plan to broadcast Hassan’s death shocked the country. President Trump rightly called it off, and the Secretary accepted the decision. That is how the chain of command is supposed to work.

Firing Mr. Hegseth would reward the people who resist reform most. A successor would face a bruising confirmation fight, and the Department would drift through months of weakened acting leadership. Every program office that dragged its feet would learn that it can outlast a reformer. Our adversaries would draw the same lesson.

Pete Hegseth has been highly effective and should remain President Trump's Secretary of War. No on impeachment.

funding.detail: Federal cards show the principal campaign committee and OpenFEC totals for one two-year cycle, plus itemized Schedule A contributors. House uses 2026.
